title: Custom software vs off-the-shelf: how to decide
excerpt: A practical framework for deciding when to build, when to buy and when to combine both.
body:
Most businesses face the same choice: buy a ready-made tool, or build something tailored. Neither is always right.

## When off-the-shelf wins
Buy when the process is common (accounting, email, basic project tracking), when you need to start this week, or when vendors already serve your industry well.

## When custom wins
Build when your process is the competitive advantage, when you pay for many unused features, when several tools must be stitched together by hand, or when per-seat pricing grows faster than your revenue.

## The hybrid path
Often the best answer is to keep proven tools for commodity needs and build only the layer that is unique to you — a customer portal, a workflow engine or a reporting dashboard connected through APIs.

## Questions to ask before deciding
- How much staff time does the current workaround cost each month?
- What happens to the data if the vendor changes pricing or shuts down?
- Who will maintain the custom system in two years?

A short discovery phase answers these questions with numbers instead of opinions.

title: What actually makes a business website rank on Google
excerpt: The technical foundations that matter before you spend a rupee on content or ads.
body:
Ranking is not a trick. It is the result of a site search engines can crawl, understand and trust.

## 1. Crawlability
Pages should be reachable through normal links, return correct status codes and be listed in an up-to-date sitemap. Blocked or orphaned pages cannot rank.

## 2. Clear structure
One topic per page, descriptive titles, a logical heading order and internal links that connect related pages.

## 3. Speed and stability
Core Web Vitals measure loading, responsiveness and layout stability on real devices. Heavy images and scripts are the usual culprits.

## 4. Structured data
Schema markup helps search engines understand what a page is — an organisation, a service, an article — and can enable richer results.

## 5. Genuinely useful content
Pages that answer a real question better than the alternatives earn links and rankings over time. Quantity without depth does not.

Fix the foundation first; every later investment in content and promotion then works harder.

title: Where AI automation pays off in a small business
excerpt: Five repetitive tasks where automation saves real time, and three where it does not.
body:
AI works best on repetitive, well-defined tasks with a person reviewing the output.

## Good candidates
- Routing and tagging incoming enquiries
- Drafting replies to common customer questions
- Extracting fields from invoices and forms
- Summarising meetings and call notes
- Producing routine reports from existing data

## Weak candidates
- Decisions with legal or safety consequences and no human review
- Tasks where the rules change daily and nobody documents them
- Anything that depends on data you do not actually have

## How to start
Pick one process, measure how long it takes today, automate a small part with a human check, and compare. Expand only when the numbers justify it.

The goal is not to replace people; it is to remove the copy-paste work that keeps them from better work.
